title: Consumers are redefining value as a hybrid bargain: fair prices, reliable quality, controlled AI and meaningful human support
source_unit: Capgemini Research Institute, What matters to today's consumer 2026
geography: Consumers aged 18 and over across Australia, Canada, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States

denominator.unit: consumers aged 18 and over across 12 countries

fair_value.value: 74% would switch brands for a lower regular price, while 71% would switch if pack size or product quality fell without clear communication

quality_boundary.value: nearly four in five avoid private labels in performance-critical categories, showing that price pressure stops where reliability or health is at stake

shrinkflation.value: 64% view shrinkflation as an unfair practice

observations.method: Capgemini Research Institute global consumer survey supplemented by interviews with consumer-products and retail executives.
observations.uncertainty: Switching intentions and fairness perceptions are self-reported; the study does not observe actual switching, category-specific household budgets or whether reliability concerns are objectively warranted.
observations.subgroup: Consumers facing inflation fatigue, private-label shoppers, buyers of performance-critical or health-related products, and brands competing on price, quality and transparency.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consumers may state that fairness and quality matter while still choosing the cheapest available option when financial room is severely constrained; stated switching can also be aspirational.

observations.period: October 2025 survey; spending restraint and emotional coping

denominator.unit: consumers aged 18 and over across 12 countries

restraint.value: 54% say they are making fewer impulse purchases, down from 71% in the prior year, while 49% are buying smaller pack sizes
restraint.unit: reported survey shares and year-over-year comparison

indulgence.value: 71% say small treats or indulgences help them manage financial stress

decision_frame.value: the report describes a hybrid mindset: consumers trade down in some categories while retaining spending where health, reliability, durability or emotional value matter

observations.method: Capgemini longitudinal consumer survey comparison and 2026 questions on spending, pack sizes, impulse behavior and emotional value.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison uses different annual waves and self-reported behavior; small indulgence may represent substitution, coping, habit or discretionary resilience rather than aggregate spending growth.
observations.subgroup: Consumers cutting nonessential spending, consumers maintaining health or reliability purchases, and households using small treats as emotional relief during financial pressure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Intentional indulgence can coexist with severe financial stress and may conceal reductions elsewhere; category-level trade-down does not indicate a uniform consumer culture.

denominator.unit: consumers aged 18 and over across 12 countries

adoption.value: 25% have used generative-AI shopping tools and a further 31% plan to use them in the future

agentic_routines.value: 52% use virtual assistants that automate reordering or meal planning at least once a week, but only one in five is willing to pay for such a service

control_and_data.value: 76% want clear rules for when an AI assistant acts and 71% are concerned about how generative AI uses their information

observations.method: Capgemini survey questions on generative-AI shopping tools, virtual assistants, permissions, data use, synthetic influencers and disclosure.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not verify tool use, distinguish embedded from standalone systems, measure task quality or establish whether concern reduces adoption over time.
observations.subgroup: Current and prospective AI-shopping users, consumers seeking convenience, people prioritizing autonomy and consumers concerned about data use, synthetic content and agentic action.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consumers may accept automated assistance when permissions are reversible and visible; concern about data use may be compatible with continued use when convenience or price benefits are high.

observations.period: 2025-2026; technology convenience, human support and social commerce

denominator.unit: consumers aged 18 and over across 12 countries

technology_benefit.value: 65% feel technology has reduced stress in their shopping routines and 63% want generative AI to provide hyper-personalized content

human_support.value: 74% value in-person assistance during in-store service and 66% during the purchase stage, up from 54% and 40% respectively in the prior year
human_support.unit: reported survey shares and year-over-year comparison

social_commerce.value: 35% have purchased through platforms such as Instagram or YouTube, while two-thirds expect brands to disclose AI-generated advertising

observations.method: Capgemini survey comparison of shopping stress, personalization, human assistance, social-commerce purchase and synthetic advertising disclosure expectations.
observations.uncertainty: The findings are perceptions and reported behavior rather than transaction records; the year-over-year increase in human-support preference may reflect question, channel or sample effects as well as changing consumer needs.
observations.subgroup: Consumers making complex purchases, shoppers using social commerce, customers needing service resolution, and consumers balancing digital convenience with interpersonal trust.
observations.counterinterpretation: Demand for human assistance may reflect the complexity or failure of current digital journeys rather than rejection of technology; social-commerce adoption does not prove durable loyalty or trust.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-value and AI-commerce layer linking inflation fatigue to fairness, quality, switching, emotional indulgence, controlled automation, data concern, human support and social commerce. It is a 12-country survey with executive interviews, not respondent-level ingestion, transaction telemetry, a causal evaluation, a complete global consumer census or proof that stated preferences become realized loyalty.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Capgemini publication page and 82-page PDF were reviewed for the 12,000-consumer methodology, fairness and switching measures, intentional-indulgence findings, AI-shopping adoption and control, data concerns, human-support comparisons and social-commerce disclosure expectations.
